newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US rates up in Q1 '97, taper off by Q4.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US rates up in Q1 '97, taper off by Q4.

text.p: Mild inflationary pressures will push U.S. long-term interest rates moderately higher for the next few quarters, but yields will begin to taper off by fourth-quarter 1997, U.S. economists said in a Reuters poll.

On average, 24 experts surveyed on Monday forecast the 30-year Treasury bond yield would hold steady at around 6.70 percent by early December, rise to as high as 6.85 by the end of second-quarter 1997, and ebb to 6.73 a year from now.

The drop in bond yields will be a direct result of a tempered easing of short-term interest rates by the central bank in the second half of 1997, according to Stuart Hoffman, chief economist for PNC Bank.
He said inflation will hold steady throughout the end of this year and into next year, but start to trail off toward the end of 1997.
"I have the Federal Reserve easing before the end of 1997 ... and as a result, when the Fed eases, short-term rates come down," said Hoffman.
David Greenlaw, an economist at Morgan Stanley and Co Inc, agreed inflationary pressures will push interest rates higher, but he did not forecast an easing by the end of next year.

"Although things look pretty sanguine right now," said Greenlaw, "we think inflation will become an issue in 1997, and the Fed is going to have to push the real (federal) funds rate further into the restrictive zone, as well as keeping pace with the underlying increase of inflation."

The result will be more tightening at the short end of the Treasury yield curve and rates rising at the long end, Greenlaw said, explaining that tight labor markets could aggravate wage pressures next year.

But recent fears of wage-push inflation dissipated after a lower-than-expected rise in the Employment Cost Index (ECI) for the third quarter. The gauge rose 0.6 percent against an expected 0.8 percent increase.
Nevertheless, many economists are calling for a hike in short-term interest rates in the near future.

"I'm hoping the economy is going to build some momentum in the next couple of months," said Christopher Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. He estimated the central bank will rein in credit by the end of March-1997.
The experts predicted the two-year note yield would move in tandem with the long bond but not falling as much, leading to a flatter yield curve.
On average, pundits projected the two-year rate would rise as high as 6.11 percent by the end of the second-quarter 1997 and retreat to 5.99 percent by the fourth quarter.
Full results of the survey follow.
